item.content:encoded:
OPINION | A woman handed a house, but denied the title deed, is not empowered - News24Aug 27, 2026

发布源: South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-08-28

The government says it wants to empower women. It could start by handing over their title deeds, writesAnlu Keevé.

Earlier this month, I took a Grade 10 pupil to an all-you-can-eat sushi buffet for her birthday. It happened to be Women’s Day.

Somewhere between the second and third plate, she told me about the janitor at her school, who was wrestling a wheelbarrow up a short flight of stairs when a female teacher offered to give him a hand. This was, he explained, a job for a man, and he preferred to go and find a man to help him.

Our discussion about this exchange took up the rest of the drive home, because it’s not a subject you can raise with a teenager on Women’s Day without setting off a long conversation about what an empowered woman is.

In fairness to the janitor, I doubt he believes women are incapable of helping to get a wheelbarrow up five steps. He was more likely trying to be courteous in the idiom most familiar to him and, as courtesies go, it is harmless enough. I have no particular wish to manhandle a wheelbarrow up any stairs myself, and I suspect the teacher’s own enthusiasm for the job was limited, but the principle survives our shared indifference: a woman who wants to do with a wheelbarrow whatever she wishes should be free to do so.

What struck me afterwards was that the janitor’s response has a much larger and far more consequential echo, and it’s an echo that rings loudest in government.

item.title: [South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa] The Hoernlé Memorial Lectures
item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
The Hoernlé Memorial Lectures

发布源: South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-08-28

The inaugural Hoernlé lecture was delivered by Jan Hendrik Hofmeyr, IRR vice-president and honorary life member, in 1945 on the topic of “Christian principles and race problems”. Other distinguished speakers included IRR co-founder Professor Edgar Brookes on the Institute’s first 21 years in “We come of age” (1950), Archbishop Dennis Hurley on “Apartheid: A crisis of the Christian conscience” (1964), Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi on “White and black nationalism, ethnicity and the future of the homelands” (1974), Dr Alan Paton on “Towards racial justice: Will there be a change of heart?” (1979) and again on “Federation or desolation” (1985) – the only speaker to have delivered two Hoernlé lectures – Professor Jonathan Jansen on “When does a university cease to exist?” (2005) and Professor RW Johnson on “The future of the liberal tradition in South Africa” (2011).

The speakers often tackled thorny questions relating to race, ideology and South Africa’s future. In their explorations, they reflected the most pressing preoccupations of their times, giving us a window into the past that shows contemporary views on issues that often seemed intractable at the time. It is sobering to look back from today’s vantage point and realise how far South Africa has come – and how much still remains to be done to create a free and prosperous South Africa for all.

item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
History of the IRR Bursary Programme (1936-2022)

发布源: South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-08-28

From a time of simple racial segregation in the first part of the twentieth century, through the intensified racial regime of the apartheid period and for nearly three decades into post-apartheid democracy, about 6,000 black South Africans graduated from universities, technikons and other tertiary institutions thanks to the bursary programme administered by the South African Institute of Race Relations (SAIRR). Immense hurdles had to be overcome, both by the students themselves as well as funders and administrators.

While unquestionably delivering positive outcomes, the programme was often caught up in the turbulence of the times, especially during the popular resistance from the mid-1970s to the early 1990s. If not itself the subject of controversy, it was often linked to controversy and conflict around matters like reform versus revolution, disinvestment versus business influence, and armed struggle versus peaceful resistance. This is the story of that bursary programme and the tumultuous times in which it operated.

The South African Institute of Race Relations (SAIRR) is a classically liberal not-for-profit organisation, founded in 1929 with the objective of improving relations between South Africa's race groups. This almost immediately became a matter of opposing racial discrimination and promoting the establishment of a non-racial society in South Africa. item.content:encoded:
African Heritage Program

发布源: Mandela Institute for Development Studies (MINDS) --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-08-28

CULTURE AND DEVELOPMENT

The African Heritage Program explores African people, culture and heritage to ground development in Africanness. Through rigorous research, it deepens the understanding of African identity and value systems to inform development practice.

FOUNDATIONAL APPROACH

MINDS believes that a better understanding of Africanness begins with systematic research and rigorous analysis of African heritage. This work seeks to develop an inclusive conceptualisation of Africanness, grounded in the values,and lived realities of African societies. Anchored in this understanding, the programme aims to inform development initiatives that are culturally grounded and more effective in addressing Africa’s development challenges.

APPLYING KNOWLEDGE

The Program identifies foundational African principles across governance, leadership and knowledge domains, applying these insights to assess and shape development initiatives.

item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在Mandela Institute for Development Studies (MINDS) --South Africa官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
Economic Integration Program

发布源: Mandela Institute for Development Studies (MINDS) --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-08-28

REGIONAL COOPERATION

Accelerating Africa’s growth requires stronger cross-sector partnerships and deeper regional integration.

PROGRAM RESPONSE

Through the Economic Integration Program, MINDS underscores the urgency of advancing integration as a driver of Africa’s development. Despite strong continental intent, fragmented markets persist, limiting growth. The program promotes practical implementation, strengthens regional value chains, and improves market access to support the shift from policy ambition to meaningful, sustained economic transformation.

APPLYING KNOWLEDGE

Through inclusive, multi-sectoral dialogues, the MINDS High-Level Dialogue Series strengthens relationships across Africa, helping leaders from all sectors create shared visions and work together to tackle the continent’s complex development issues.
